metadata.title: Corneal Edema and Opacification Preferred Practice Pattern®
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the evaluation and management of corneal edema and corneal opacification in patients of any age. It covers causes, visual and functional assessment, diagnostic testing, optical and medical care, and surgical options selected according to the affected corneal layers and the patient's needs. It also discusses complications, follow-up, counseling, and referral.

target_population: Individuals of any age with corneal edema or opacification

associated_therapies: Topical or systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
recognition: Corneal thickening, epithelial microcysts, stromal edema or reduced corneal clarity may be apparent on examination.
prevention: When endothelial dysfunction might contribute to edema, topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors should not be the initial treatment for elevated intraocular pressure.
Avoid inadvertent corneal contact with topical Chlorhexidine during facial surgical preparation.

toxicities.event: Rho kinase inhibitor-associated corneal and ocular adverse effects
recognition: A honey-comb pattern of corneal edema, pain, conjunctival hyperemia or cornea verticillate may develop; these effects are often reversible.

toxicities.event: Elevated intraocular pressure associated with corticosteroids
recognition: Intraocular pressure may rise during treatment.

management.severity: Steroid use when treating corneal inflammation
management.actions: Arrange follow-up to identify a pressure response to corticosteroids and associated intraocular pressure elevation.

prevention: Monitor intraocular pressure during prolonged topical corticosteroid treatment.

recognition: Cataract may develop during long-term treatment.
prevention: Monitor for cataract formation with prolonged topical corticosteroid use.

toxicities.event: Infectious keratitis associated with a bandage contact lens
recognition: New redness, pain or increased photophobia during lens wear warrants contact with the treating ophthalmologist.
prevention: Consider a prophylactic broad-spectrum topical antibiotic when a BCL is used, while recognizing that antibiotics may not eliminate infection risk.
Prefer a limited treatment period; if extended wear is necessary, exchange the lens periodically, generally before the same lens has remained on the eye longer than one month.
Provide regular follow-up to examine the lens and ocular status, and counsel patients about symptoms requiring prompt contact.

toxicities.event: Corneal melt or perforation associated with topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drops
recognition: Corneal melting or perforation is a concern after epithelial debridement.
prevention: If a short postoperative course is used for discomfort, provide close follow-up.

recognition: Potential effects include keratocyte depletion, endothelial failure and limbal stem cell deficiency.
prevention: Verify pharmacy preparation of the intended dose and carefully control exposure time.
Definitive criteria for use, optimal dose, application method and exposure period in corneal disorders have not been established.

toxicities.event: Necrosis or corneal melt after intentional surface scarification
recognition: Excessive treatment can lead to corneal necrosis or melting.
prevention: Avoid overtreatment when performing scarification for painful bullous keratopathy.

recognition: The postoperative hyperopic shift is greater after DSAEK than after DMEK; tissue removal during PTK can also flatten the cornea and produce hyperopia.

management.severity: Cataract surgery when subsequent endothelial keratoplasty is likely
management.actions: Consider the expected refractive change when selecting IOL power and discuss the choice and possible later corneal decompensation with the patient.

prevention: For PTK, peripheral small-spot ablations or a refractive setting may lessen the induced refractive change.

toxicities.event: Postkeratectomy haze, scarring or recurrent deposits
recognition: Haze may be temporary, whereas scarring can cause lasting visual effects; recurrence of the original disease or stromal deposits may also occur.
Risk factors for scarring include dystrophies, delayed re-epithelialization and ablation deeper than 50 to 75µm.

management.severity: Recurrent disease or opacity after PTK

prevention: Adjunctive intraoperative MMC may be helpful when postoperative anti-inflammatory treatment is insufficient to prevent scarring.
MMC has been investigated to limit recurrent scar tissue or stromal deposits.

recognition: Risk is particularly noted when ablation extends beyond the anterior third of the corneal stroma or the remaining stromal bed measures less than 250 µm.

toxicities.event: Delayed epithelial healing after corneal procedures
recognition: Persistence of an epithelial defect may complicate healing; underlying conditions requiring keratectomy can themselves contribute.

management.actions: Autologous serum or an amniotic membrane may be used to assist epithelial repair.

prevention: Before corneal transplantation, address eyelid abnormalities, infection, inflammation and ocular surface disease where possible.

toxicities.event: Delayed healing and infection risk after EDTA chelation
recognition: Mean epithelial healing after chelation may take 5–7 days, compared with 2–3 days for a similar-sized abrasion in a normal eye; slower repair increases the risk of stromal scarring and infection.

management.severity: Coexisting limbal stem cell deficiency, neurotrophic keratopathy or severe dry eye
management.actions: Amniotic membrane grafting or temporary tarsorrhaphy may aid re-epithelialization. With severe ocular surface disease, keratectomy risks may outweigh its benefits.

prevention: Avoid limbal exposure to EDTA and minimize exposure where possible.

toxicities.event: Graft dislocation or detachment after endothelial keratoplasty
toxicities.incidence: In the comparison for Fuchs dystrophy and pseudophakic bullous keratopathy, the dislocation rate was 14.5%94–15%97 for DSAEK and 5.9%-27.4%98, 99 for DMEK; the PK comparator was 0.0%. The DSAEK footnote states that counting all dislocations, rather than only those affecting the result, yields 8.0%–24.0%.
recognition: Early DMEK separation involving more than 30% of total graft area predicts persistent or complete detachment more strongly than separation involving less than 30%, which tends to reattach completely.
Anterior segment optical coherence tomography can identify regions where donor tissue does not adhere.

management.actions: Recentring or rebubbling may be necessary in the office or operating room.

prevention: During DMEK, an “S” stamp or another orientation mark and SF6 gas have significantly lowered iatrogenic primary graft failure and rebubbling rates.

toxicities.incidence: For donor failure within 60 days, the surgical comparison reports 0.3%102 for PK, 0%–29.0%; mean 5.0%94, 103 for DSAEK, and 2.2%–8.0%103-105 for DMEK.
recognition: Donor cornea does not clear during the first 8 weeks after surgery, without another explanation for stromal edema such as an epithelial defect, elevated intraocular pressure, rejection or inflammation.
prevention: Avoid excessive manipulation or trauma to donor tissue.
For DMEK, orientation marking and SF6 gas have significantly reduced iatrogenic primary failure.

toxicities.incidence: In patients with Fuchs dystrophy and pseudophakic bullous keratopathy, registry data reported 13% rejection over 1 year after PK. A DSAEK study reported 6.0%, 14.0%, and 22.0% at 1, 2, and 3 years, respectively; another reported 7.6% at 1 year and 12.0% at 2 years. Overall allograft rejection was 1.9% after DALK versus 7.8% after PK. Stromal rejection following DALK was reported between 2% and 12%. Two studies directly comparing PK with DSAEK for Fuchs dystrophy and pseudophakic bullous keratopathy found no statistically significant difference in rejection rates; large-cohort reports describe a significantly lower rejection risk with DMEK than with both PK and DSAEK.
recognition: Rejection may affect full-thickness or partial-thickness grafts.
Stromal rejection can occur after DALK, but endothelial rejection does not occur with that procedure.

management.actions: Early, intensive topical, periocular and systemic corticosteroid treatment may reverse the reaction.
Topical corticosteroids can usually reverse rejection.

prevention: Long-term topical corticosteroids may lower rejection risk, with surveillance for steroid-related pressure elevation and infectious keratitis.
After PK, patients at high risk or with recurrent inflammation may require augmentation of standard treatment with higher daily corticosteroid doses or oral antiviral agents.
Identify and address preoperative factors that impair graft survival, including deep stromal vascularization and ocular surface disease.

recognition: Perforation may occur while separating Descemet’s membrane from overlying stroma and is more likely with a deep scar, scarring involving the membrane or a history of membrane rupture.

management.actions: The DALK procedure may be completed.
Conversion to PK may be necessary.

toxicities.event: Double anterior chamber or delayed Descemet’s membrane detachment after DALK
recognition: If lamellar surgery continues despite a larger Descemet’s membrane perforation, fluid may collect between the membrane and graft.
Delayed detachment may also occur as endothelium repopulates the posterior cornea or traction develops with progressive fibrosis.
Infection can follow disruption of the epithelial barrier, a nonhealing epithelium, suture problems or organisms sequestered at a graft interface.
Herpes virus should be considered in the differential diagnosis after excimer laser exposure, corticosteroid use or corneal trauma.

management.actions: Surgical treatment is generally needed for multiple interface infiltrates; options described are donor-button exchange or PK.

prevention: A history of herpetic eye disease warrants strong consideration of perioperative antiviral prophylaxis.

toxicities.incidence: Table 6 reports 6.1%–12.5% endophthalmitis after Boston keratoprosthesis.
recognition: After transplantation, possible sources include periocular organisms, postoperative ocular-surface or interface defects, donor tissue and storage media.
After BKPro, compromised structural integrity can predispose to vision-threatening infection.

management.actions: Management depends on clinical findings rather than donor-rim culture results alone.

prevention: Lifelong antimicrobial prophylaxis is recommended after BKPro.

Sharing positive fungal donor-rim culture results with the originating eye bank enables closer monitoring of the recipient of the paired tissue; there is no consensus on prophylactic antifungal treatment after a positive culture.

toxicities.event: Glaucoma or progression of glaucoma after keratoprosthesis
toxicities.incidence: The clinical discussion states that 72% to 89% have glaucoma before keratoprosthesis placement, 14% to 36% develop glaucoma, and 13% to 33% have progression. Table 6 reports pre-existing glaucoma in 72.0%–86.0% and new or progressive glaucoma in 14%–39.3%. One report found progression as low as 2% with 17 months of follow-up when tube-shunt surgery preceded or accompanied implantation in eyes with poorly controlled intraocular pressure; other reports found rates as high as 38%, particularly when additional comorbidities were included.
recognition: Intraocular pressure cannot be measured reliably after implantation.
Progressive angle closure and chronic intraocular inflammation are contributing causes.

management.actions: Aim for a low pressure as assessed by finger palpation, and reassess the optic nerve and visual fields to monitor progression.

prevention: Tube-shunt surgery before or at the time of implantation has been studied in eyes with poorly controlled intraocular pressure.

toxicities.incidence: 14%–29.5% in Table 6 for the listed vitreoretinal complications collectively.
recognition: The listed complications include detachments, hemorrhage, cystoid macular edema, choroidal effusion, epiretinal membrane, vitreous hemorrhage, vitritis and choroidal detachment.

management.actions: Care of BKPro patients may involve glaucoma and retina specialists.

recognition: The permanent junction of living tissue and the prosthetic optic can contribute to epithelial defects that do not heal.
prevention: Therapeutic soft BCLs are routinely used to reduce ocular-surface microtrauma and desiccation.
Optimization of the ocular surface before BKPro with limbal stem cell transplantation, mucous membrane grafting or amniotic membranes may be beneficial.

recognition: The interface between the prosthetic material and biological tissue can develop sterile necrosis and perforation.
prevention: Therapeutic soft BCLs are routinely used to limit microtrauma and desiccation and improve device retention.

toxicities.event: Uveitis or sterile vitritis after keratoprosthesis

recognition: Possible fungal infiltrates on a therapeutic contact lens or beside the prosthesis stem require immediate attention.

management.actions: Immediately discontinue topical corticosteroids and use natamycin 5%, amphotericin B, or voriconazole 1%.

prevention: Use lifelong antimicrobial prophylaxis after BKPro.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Consider a prophylactic broad-spectrum topical antibiotic when using a BCL; counsel that antibiotics may not fully prevent infection.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients wearing a BCL for corneal edema or epithelial disease

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use an antibiotic drop or ointment to protect a persistent epithelial defect; select the agent with regard to ocular and periocular flora, contact lens history, immune status and underlying illness.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with a corneal epithelial defect

prophylaxis.recommendation: Topical antibiotics are often applied following epithelial debridement.
Give strong consideration to antiviral prophylaxis because herpes virus may reactivate following excimer laser exposure, corticosteroid use or corneal trauma.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with a history of herpetic eye disease undergoing a corneal procedure

prophylaxis.recommendation: Long-term topical corticosteroids may reduce rejection risk, but monitor for steroid-related intraocular pressure elevation and infectious keratitis.
Standard post-PK treatment may need higher daily corticosteroid doses or oral antiviral agents.
prophylaxis.target_population: PK recipients at high risk or with recurrent inflammation, including herpes simplex virus keratitis, herpes zoster ophthalmicus or uveitis

prophylaxis.recommendation: Adjunctive intraoperative MMC can be helpful when postoperative anti-inflammatory treatment may not adequately prevent corneal scarring; its optimal dose and application have not been established for corneal disorders.
prophylaxis.target_population: Selected patients undergoing superficial or anterior lamellar keratectomy

prophylaxis.recommendation: For a typical BKPro, use daily polymyxin B combined with trimethoprim or a fourth-generation fluoroquinolone, with or without vancomycin.
Use daily dual coverage with vancomycin combined with polymyxin B/trimethoprim or a fourth-generation fluoroquinolone, or daily fluoroquinolone with chloramphenicol.
prophylaxis.target_population: BKPro recipients with an autoimmune condition and/or monocular patients

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Secondary bacterial infection of a persistent epithelial defect
infection_management.prevention: An antibiotic drop or ointment is conventionally used; selection takes account of periocular flora, contact lens wear, immune status and underlying medical conditions.

Consider a broad-spectrum topical antibiotic, limit lens wear where possible, exchange lenses periodically during extended treatment and provide regular follow-up; one study suggested increased infectious keratitis risk with BCLs and indicated that antibiotics might not prevent it.
infection_management.management: Advise patients to contact their treating ophthalmologist if redness, pain or increased photophobia occurs.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Herpetic keratitis reactivation after a corneal procedure
infection_management.prevention: A history of herpetic eye disease warrants strong consideration of perioperative antiviral prophylaxis.
infection_management.management: Include herpes virus in the differential diagnosis of postoperative infectious keratitis.
Surgery is generally necessary for multiple interface infiltrates; the donor button can be replaced or PK performed.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Recurrent Acanthamoeba keratitis after therapeutic DALK
infection_management.prevention: Measures described to avoid recurrence include confocal microscopy or creating a wide margin around affected cornea.
infection_management.management: Recurrence was observed in 20% of cases in the cited experience; the guideline does not specify a treatment for recurrence.

infection_management.prevention: Fungal donor-rim cultures may be considered, and positive results should be shared with the source eye bank to permit closer monitoring of the paired-tissue recipient. There is no consensus on preventive antifungal treatment after a positive fungal culture.
infection_management.management: Base management on clinical signs of endophthalmitis; donor-rim cultures alone do not determine treatment.

infection_management.prevention: Lifelong antimicrobial prophylaxis is recommended because compromise of ocular integrity can lead to vision-threatening infection.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Suspected fungal infiltrates associated with BKPro
infection_management.management: If infiltrates are suspected on the therapeutic contact lens or alongside the prosthesis stem, immediately stop topical corticosteroids and use natamycin 5%, amphotericin B, or voriconazole 1%.

therapies_index.name: topical sodium chloride 5%
therapies_index.mechanism: Produces a hyperosmotic effect.
approved_indications: Temporary management of primary or secondary corneal edema.
therapies_index.administration: Topical drops or ointment; discontinue after a number of weeks if no benefit is observed.
monitoring: Assess whether vision or symptoms improve.

therapies_index.name: hairdryer
therapies_index.mechanism: Produces a hyperosmotic effect.
approved_indications: Temporary management of primary or secondary corneal edema.
therapies_index.administration: Discontinue after a number of weeks if no benefit is observed.
monitoring: Assess whether vision or symptoms improve.

therapies_index.name: Rho kinase inhibitors
approved_indications: May have a role in reducing edema associated with Fuchs corneal dystrophy; efficacy and safety require randomized controlled trials.

therapies_index.name: Rho kinase inhibitor
approved_indications: May be used topically with primary descemetorhexis to facilitate endothelial health in selected patients with Fuchs.
therapies_index.administration: Topical use with primary descemetorhexis is described.

therapies_index.name: prostaglandin analogues
key_toxicities: Potential inflammatory effect; avoid when inflammation may contribute to corneal edema.

therapies_index.name: topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
therapies_index.mechanism: May interfere with the endothelial pump.
key_toxicities: Potential interference with endothelial function; should not be first-line treatment when endothelial dysfunction may contribute to edema.

therapies_index.name: topical corticosteroid
therapies_index.mechanism: Reduces corneal and intraocular inflammation.
approved_indications: Control of inflammation contributing to corneal edema after possible infection has been excluded or controlled.
Supportive treatment of acute hydrops.
Treatment of corneal transplant rejection.
therapies_index.administration: Topical; long-term treatment may be used after corneal transplantation.
key_toxicities: Infectious keratitis during long-term post-transplant use
monitoring: Follow up for steroid responsiveness and elevated IOP.
Monitor IOP and cataract formation during long-term use.
Monitor for infectious keratitis during long-term post-transplant use.

therapies_index.name: cycloplegic agents
approved_indications: Supportive treatment of inflammation or pain in acute hydrops.
monitoring: Monitor improvement and resolution of edema in acute hydrops.

therapies_index.name: hyperosmotic drops and ointments
approved_indications: Supportive treatment of acute hydrops.
therapies_index.administration: Topical drops or ointments.
monitoring: Monitor improvement and resolution of edema in acute hydrops.

therapies_index.name: topical antibiotics
approved_indications: May reduce secondary infection when corneal bullae rupture.
Protection against secondary bacterial infection in an epithelial defect.
Supportive treatment of acute hydrops.
Prophylaxis after epithelial debridement.
therapies_index.administration: Topical drops or ointment are described for epithelial defects.
monitoring: Monitor improvement and resolution of edema in acute hydrops.

therapies_index.name: topical prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotic
approved_indications: Consider to reduce secondary infection risk when a bandage contact lens is used; antibiotics may not eliminate infectious keratitis risk.
therapies_index.administration: Topical during bandage contact lens use.
monitoring: Watch for redness, pain, or increased photophobia during bandage contact lens wear.

therapies_index.name: preservative-free artificial tears
therapies_index.mechanism: May provide enough lubrication for a bandage contact lens to move on blinking.
approved_indications: Concomitant dry eye when movement of a bandage contact lens is inadequate.

therapies_index.name: bandage contact lens (BCL)
therapies_index.mechanism: Protects the ocular surface and can alleviate discomfort from epithelial disease.
approved_indications: Pain or discomfort from microcystic or bullous epithelial disease.
Delayed epithelial healing.
Protection and comfort after corneal tissue adhesive or epithelial debridement.
therapies_index.administration: A thin, high-water-content lens with high oxygen diffusion is considered safest; a relatively flat fit with movement on blinking is generally desirable. Ideally use for a limited period, exchange periodically if longer use is required, and in most cases do not leave the same lens in place longer than one month.
key_toxicities: Potential trauma to an edematous epithelium in severe cases
monitoring: Arrange regular follow-up to reassess lens fit and ocular status.
Advise prompt contact with the treating ophthalmologist for redness, pain, or increased photophobia.

therapies_index.name: scleral lenses
therapies_index.mechanism: Provide a more regular optical surface.
approved_indications: Improvement of vision and symptoms when advanced edema or scarring makes other contact lenses difficult to fit.
Correction of vision affected by corneal surface irregularity when greater lens stability is needed.

therapies_index.name: RGP lens
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates a smoother refractive surface over corneal irregularity.
approved_indications: Visual improvement when surface irregularity contributes substantially to impairment from corneal opacification.

therapies_index.name: hybrid lens
approved_indications: Visual improvement when corneal irregularity is important and greater lens stability is needed.

therapies_index.name: painted contact lenses
therapies_index.mechanism: Conceal a visible corneal opacity.
approved_indications: Cosmetic concealment of an opacity when visual potential is poor.
A clear pupillary zone with an opaque periphery is available for peripheral opacities.

therapies_index.name: scleral shells
therapies_index.mechanism: Conceal a corneal opacity.
approved_indications: Cosmetic concealment when visual potential is poor, particularly with reduced orbital volume or phthisis bulbi.

therapies_index.name: intraocular gas
therapies_index.mechanism: Helps close the endothelial break and reduce corneal edema.
approved_indications: May hasten resolution of acute hydrops.
therapies_index.administration: Placed intraocularly.

therapies_index.name: anterior stromal puncture
therapies_index.mechanism: Intentionally scars the anterior cornea to reduce bullae formation and pain.
approved_indications: Painful longstanding bullous keratopathy when visual rehabilitation is not the principal objective.
therapies_index.administration: Performed with electrocautery or a needle.
key_toxicities: Excessive scarification can cause necrosis and corneal melt.

therapies_index.name: PTK
therapies_index.mechanism: Excimer laser ablation removes superficial corneal tissue; ablation of the sub-basal nerve plexis has been proposed to account for pain relief.
approved_indications: Reduction of pain and improvement of surface stability in corneal edema, without long-term visual rehabilitation.
Removal or smoothing of superficial and anterior stromal opacities.
Management of band keratopathy.
May postpone DALK or PK for granular and lattice corneal dystrophies.
therapies_index.administration: For pain and surface stability, ablations to a depth of 100 µm or greater have been used alone or with self-retaining amniotic membrane grafts. Masking agents may fill surface depressions during treatment.
key_toxicities: Corneal ectasia, particularly when ablation exceeds the anterior third of corneal stroma or the residual stromal bed is less than 250 µm
monitoring: Follow epithelial healing and watch for infection.

therapies_index.name: annular keratotomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Corneal trephination to a mid-stromal depth is used to obtain pain relief.
approved_indications: Pain associated with corneal edema.
therapies_index.administration: Performed as an annular cut to mid-stromal depth.

therapies_index.name: conjunctival flap
therapies_index.mechanism: Covers the cornea to facilitate healing and comfort and reduce inflammation.
approved_indications: Persistent discomfort from corneal edema when visual potential is limited or absent.
Definitive treatment when further reconstruction is not planned, or interim treatment before more definitive therapy.
therapies_index.administration: A full conjunctival flap (Gundersen) is among the described approaches.

therapies_index.name: amniotic membrane transplant
therapies_index.mechanism: An inlay provides a scaffold for migrating epithelial cells; an overlay provides a protective patch beneath which epithelium heals.
approved_indications: Persistent discomfort from corneal edema when visual potential is limited or absent.
Support of healing in persistent epithelial defects or impaired re-epithelialization.
therapies_index.administration: The membrane may be placed as an inlay, a sutured overlay, or a self-retaining onlay under a therapeutic lens or on a scleral ring.

therapies_index.name: EK
therapies_index.mechanism: Replaces diseased endothelial tissue while retaining anterior corneal layers.
approved_indications: Preferred corneal transplantation approach for endothelial failure without corneal scarring.
monitoring: Assess donor adherence and graft position after surgery.
Monitor for rejection and elevated IOP.

therapies_index.name: DMEK
therapies_index.mechanism: Exchanges the recipient's diseased Descemet’s membrane and endothelium for donor Descemet’s membrane and endothelium.
approved_indications: Mild to moderate corneal edema and standard endothelial failure when anterior chamber visibility is good.
May also be considered in eyes with decreased anterior chamber visibility or complex anatomy.
therapies_index.administration: Donor tissue is unfolded, centered, and attached using a bubble; orientation marking and SF6 gas are described.
monitoring: Assess early graft adherence; detachment involving more than 30% of total graft area predicts persistent or complete detachment relative to detachment involving less than 30%.
Monitor graft position and IOP after surgery.

therapies_index.name: DSAEK
therapies_index.mechanism: Replaces recipient Descemet’s membrane with a donor lenticule containing posterior stroma and Descemet’s membrane.
approved_indications: Endothelial failure, including eyes with reduced anterior chamber visibility or complex findings such as previous glaucoma surgery or iris defects.
May be used to regraft a PK with endothelial decompensation.
therapies_index.administration: Donor tissue is generally precut with a microkeratome; its posterior lenticule may induce hyperopic shift.
key_toxicities: Interface opacity or wrinkling that can reduce correctable distance visual acuity
monitoring: Assess graft attachment and position.
Monitor for rejection and elevated IOP.

therapies_index.name: DSEK
therapies_index.mechanism: Replaces removed recipient Descemet’s membrane with donor tissue containing posterior stroma and Descemet’s membrane.
approved_indications: Endothelial failure.
therapies_index.administration: Donor tissue is usually prepared manually by the surgeon; account for a potential hyperopic shift if cataract surgery precedes DSEK.

therapies_index.name: DLEK
therapies_index.mechanism: Replaces a posterior stromal/Descemet’s membrane lenticule.
approved_indications: Historical endothelial keratoplasty approach for corneal decompensation.
key_toxicities: Optical imperfections at the stromal interface

therapies_index.name: ultrathin DSAEK
approved_indications: Endothelial keratoplasty using tissue defined as <100 µm thick; some visual-recovery benefit versus standard DSAEK has been reported, with similar complication rates and refractive outcomes.
therapies_index.administration: Uses donor tissue <100 µm thick.

therapies_index.name: nanothin DSAEK
approved_indications: Endothelial keratoplasty using tissue defined as <50 µm thick; it may achieve results similar to DMEK.
therapies_index.administration: Uses donor tissue <50 µm thick.

therapies_index.name: DSO/DWEK
therapies_index.mechanism: Removes centrally diseased Descemet’s membrane and endothelium without donor transplantation.
approved_indications: Selected patients with Fuchs and focal central pathology with a peripheral endothelial cell count of at least 1,000 cells/sq mm; successful use is described for Fuchs but not PBK.
therapies_index.administration: Remove a 4 to 5 mm central area, with or without a topical Rho kinase inhibitor; visual rehabilitation takes up to 6 weeks.
monitoring: Follow corneal clearance; a cited small study found that allele repeats could not predict time to clearance.

therapies_index.name: PK
therapies_index.mechanism: Replaces the full thickness of the cornea.
approved_indications: Corneal edema with reduced vision or substantial pain from bullous keratopathy when full-thickness transplantation is appropriate.
Visual rehabilitation for corneal opacity.
Restoration of structural support in a thin or perforated cornea.
therapies_index.administration: Full-thickness donor corneal graft.
monitoring: Monitor graft clarity, sutures, ocular surface, rejection, infection, and IOP.

therapies_index.name: ALK (ALTK)
approved_indications: Anterior lamellar corneal replacement; therapeutic grafting can provide structural support after corneal melting or peripheral ectasia with excessive thinning or a descemetocele.
therapies_index.administration: Central grafts are generally circular; peripheral defects may require an annular or partial crescentic graft.

therapies_index.name: DALK
therapies_index.mechanism: Removes all or nearly all corneal stroma while preserving recipient Descemet’s membrane and endothelium.
approved_indications: Visual rehabilitation for deep stromal opacity or scarring and corneal ectasia.
Keratolysis associated with ocular surface disease or infectious keratitis.
therapies_index.administration: Posterior stroma may be separated with the Melles stromal pocket, Anwar’s big-bubble technique, or manual dissection; donor fixation uses sutures.
key_toxicities: Descemet’s membrane perforation or delayed detachment
monitoring: Monitor epithelial and interface healing, infection, graft survival, and stromal rejection.

therapies_index.name: FALK
therapies_index.administration: Uses a femtosecond laser for anterior lamellar keratoplasty.

therapies_index.name: FLAK/FLEK
approved_indications: Laser-assisted corneal transplantation; studies described less early postoperative astigmatism than conventional PK, without a significant difference by 6 months.
therapies_index.administration: A femtosecond laser trephines donor and recipient corneas; described incision patterns include top-hat, mushroom, and zigzag.

therapies_index.name: SK
approved_indications: Surgical treatment of selected superficial corneal opacities.
key_toxicities: Postoperative haze or scarring may follow superficial keratectomy.

therapies_index.name: epithelial debridement
therapies_index.mechanism: Removes abnormal epithelium to expose a smooth Bowman’s layer.
approved_indications: Lesions anterior to Bowman’s layer, including epithelial basement membrane dystrophy and recurrent erosions.
Symptomatic band keratopathy with glare, visual disability, or pain due to epithelial disruption.
therapies_index.administration: Remove epithelium until smooth, shiny Bowman’s layer is exposed; a therapeutic bandage contact lens and prophylactic topical antibiotics are often applied afterward.
monitoring: Follow epithelial healing.

therapies_index.name: corneal burr
therapies_index.mechanism: Smooths an irregular stromal surface.
approved_indications: Subepithelial fibrosis when debridement leaves stromal irregularity or a lesion is highly adherent.

therapies_index.name: EDTA
therapies_index.mechanism: Chelates corneal calcium deposits.
approved_indications: Removal of finer deposits in symptomatic band keratopathy after epithelial debridement.
therapies_index.administration: Applied during corneal chelation; treatment time and concentration vary with calcium density and technique.
key_toxicities: Delayed epithelial healing after chelation may increase the risk of stromal scarring and infection.
monitoring: Monitor re-epithelialization and infection.

therapies_index.name: topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAID) drops
approved_indications: A short course can help control discomfort after epithelial debridement.
therapies_index.administration: Short topical course.
monitoring: Close follow-up after use.

therapies_index.name: MMC
therapies_index.mechanism: An alkylating agent that inhibits cellular activation and proliferation during surgical wound healing.
approved_indications: Off-label adjunct to prevent or treat corneal scarring or haze when risk is high following superficial or anterior lamellar keratectomy.
May be used for recurrent subepithelial fibrosis.
therapies_index.administration: Intraoperative adjunct; the guide does not establish definitive dose, exposure period, or method for corneal disorders.
key_toxicities: Epithelial surface toxicity associated with commonly used doses in the agents discussed
monitoring: Verify pharmacy formulation and closely control exposure time.

therapies_index.name: methylcellulose
therapies_index.mechanism: Masks depressions in an irregular corneal surface during laser ablation.
approved_indications: Smoothing of the refractive surface during PTK for irregular anterior corneal lesions.
therapies_index.administration: Applied to surface depressions during PTK.

therapies_index.name: sodium hyaluronate
therapies_index.mechanism: Masks depressions in an irregular corneal surface during laser ablation.
approved_indications: Smoothing of the refractive surface during PTK for irregular anterior corneal lesions.
therapies_index.administration: Applied to surface depressions during PTK.

approved_indications: Corneal healing in nonhealing epithelial defects associated with neurotrophic keratopathy; higher healing rates than vehicle were reported.

May facilitate re-epithelialization after treatment of band keratopathy in eyes with concomitant ocular surface conditions.
therapies_index.administration: Performed with botulinum toxin or suture.

therapies_index.name: botulinum toxin
approved_indications: Can be used to produce a temporary tarsorrhaphy when blinking or eyelid closure is inadequate.
therapies_index.administration: Used for temporary tarsorrhaphy.

therapies_index.name: tissue adhesive
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides structural support or temporarily seals a small corneal defect.
approved_indications: Progressive corneal thinning, early descemetocele, or small perforation.

therapies_index.name: cyanoacrylate

monitoring: Assess for persistent leakage or secondary infection.

therapies_index.name: fibrin glue

therapies_index.administration: Should not be used for corneal perforations or descemetoceles.

therapies_index.name: corneal tattooing

therapies_index.administration: Embedded in anterior or mid corneal stroma.

approved_indications: Cosmetic treatment of corneal leukomas or occlusion of visually significant iris defects.
therapies_index.administration: Embedded in anterior or mid corneal stroma.

therapies_index.name: crescentic patch grafts
therapies_index.mechanism: Replace or reinforce damaged peripheral corneal tissue.

therapies_index.administration: A partial- or full-thickness peripheral graft may be used.

therapies_index.name: rotational autografts

approved_indications: Selected central corneal scars.
therapies_index.administration: Rotate an ipsilateral full-thickness graft while keeping the graft-host junction away from the pupil.
key_toxicities: Visual distortion if the graft-host junction is too close to the pupil

therapies_index.name: temporary keratoprosthesis
therapies_index.mechanism: Temporarily replaces an opaque cornea to provide a view for vitreoretinal surgery.
approved_indications: Vitreoretinal repair when corneal opacity prevents safe visualization.
therapies_index.administration: Insert a temporary plastic or silicone corneal device for the vitreoretinal procedure, then remove it and place a full-thickness corneal graft.

therapies_index.name: autokeratoplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Transplants clear cornea from the patient's blind eye to the eye with an opacity and visual potential.
approved_indications: Selected functionally monocular patients.
therapies_index.administration: Transfer cornea from the blind eye to the eye with visual potential.

therapies_index.name: BKPro
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides a central prosthetic optic carried by a full-thickness corneal graft.
approved_indications: An option for visual rehabilitation when other corneal transplantation approaches are unsuitable, including severe bilateral corneal blindness after multiple failed grafts.

The guide also describes use after ocular trauma and in herpetic keratitis, aniridia, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, limbal stem cell deficiency, silicone oil filled eyes, neurotrophic keratopathy, and extensive corneal neovascularization.
therapies_index.administration: A central PMMA optic is selected in 1 diopter increments according to recipient axial length; lifelong antimicrobial prophylaxis and routine therapeutic soft bandage contact lens use are described.
monitoring: Monitor ocular surface integrity and infection.
Reassess optic nerve and visual fields.
Use a low IOP target assessed by finger palpation because IOP measurement is unreliable after implantation.

therapies_index.name: Boston type 2 keratoprosthetic
therapies_index.mechanism: Places a prosthetic optic through the eyelid after complete tarsorrhaphy.
approved_indications: May be an alternative when advanced ocular surface compromise makes the BKPro type 1 unsuitable.
therapies_index.administration: Perform complete tarsorrhaphy with the PMMA optic projecting through the eyelid.

therapies_index.name: osteo-odonto-keratoprosthesis
approved_indications: Implantation with some reported success in Stevens-Johnson syndrome and OMMP.

therapies_index.name: limbal stem cell transplantation

approved_indications: May improve ocular surface condition before BKPro implantation.
therapies_index.administration: Before BKPro implantation.

therapies_index.name: mucous membrane grafting
therapies_index.mechanism: Helps optimize a compromised ocular surface.
approved_indications: May be beneficial before BKPro implantation.
therapies_index.administration: Before BKPro implantation.

therapies_index.administration: Use promptly with discontinuation of topical corticosteroids when such infiltrates are suspected.
