Rho kinase inhibitors may reduce edema in Fuchs corneal dystrophy, but randomized trials are needed to establish safety and efficacy; reported effects include often-reversible honey-comb patterned edema, pain, conjunctival hyperemia, and cornea verticillate. Lowering IOP may help if it is elevated or near the high end of normal. Avoid prostaglandin analogues when inflammation might contribute. Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors should not be first-line treatment when endothelial dysfunction may contribute. Treat inflammation with a topical corticosteroid after possible infection has been excluded or controlled, and follow up for steroid response and IOP elevation. Painful microcystic or bullous epithelium may warrant a BCL. Thin lenses with high water content and oxygen diffusion are considered safest; a relatively flat lens that moves with blinking is generally desirable, with preservative-free artificial tears if coexisting dry eye restricts movement. Consider prophylactic topical broad-spectrum antibiotics with a BCL, while recognizing that a study suggested increased infectious keratitis risk and that antibiotics may not prevent it. Explain warning symptoms of redness, pain, or increasing photophobia. Prefer a limited BCL course; if longer use is necessary, exchange lenses periodically, generally not leaving the same lens in place longer than one month, and arrange regular review. A therapeutic bandage soft lens is generally not a durable solution for edema. Severe edema or scarring can make soft or RGP fitting traumatic or difficult; scleral lenses may improve symptoms, vision, and assessment of visual potential. In acute hydrops, supportive options include topical corticosteroids, cycloplegic agents, hyperosmotic preparations, and/or antibiotics while monitoring resolution. Intraocular gas may accelerate edema resolution and closure of the endothelial break. Acute perforation may require surgery.

document_sections.heading: Surgical Management of Corneal Edema
document_sections.content: When visual rehabilitation is not intended, painful bullous keratopathy may be treated by deliberately creating a stabilizing surface scar. Anterior stromal puncture using electrocautery or a needle has been reported effective, but excessive scarification can cause necrosis and corneal melt. Several keratectomy and keratoplasty approaches can address persistent edema; TABLE 2 identifies commonly used procedures and acronyms.

document_sections.heading: Phototherapeutic Keratectomy
document_sections.content: Excimer laser PTK with ablation to a depth of 100 µm or greater, alone or with a self-retaining amniotic membrane, has been used for pain reduction and surface stabilization. Proposed pain relief involves ablation of the sub-basal nerve plexus. Mid-stromal annular keratotomy is a less involved alternative directed at the same goal. PTK for edema does not provide lasting visual rehabilitation.

document_sections.heading: Conjunctival Flap
document_sections.content: A conjunctival flap can promote rapid healing and comfort while reducing ocular inflammation. A full Gundersen flap often provides definitive treatment when later reconstruction is not planned; a flap can also quiet the eye before subsequent definitive therapy.

document_sections.heading: Amniotic Membrane Tissue Transplantation
document_sections.content: An inlay amniotic membrane supports migration of epithelial cells and may remain as a barrier against new bullae. An overlay acts as a temporary biologic contact lens while epithelium heals beneath it, then resorbs. Self-retaining onlay forms can be placed beneath a therapeutic lens or secured to a scleral ring without sutures in an office setting. Patients with persistent discomfort and limited or absent visual potential are generally better candidates for a conjunctival flap, amniotic membrane transplantation, or scarification. Some patients with useful vision choose these options because health, transportation, or follow-up constraints affect care.

document_sections.heading: Corneal Transplantation
document_sections.content: PK and lamellar transplantation, including DSAEK and DMEK, are common choices for edema with reduced vision or substantial bullous keratopathy pain. Patient-reported outcomes identified lower preoperative visual acuity and functioning, younger age, and male gender as factors affecting postkeratoplasty success (II++, Moderate, Strong). Selection of full-thickness versus lamellar surgery depends on stromal or subepithelial scarring, ocular surface healing, anterior-segment anatomy, and any necessary intraocular reconstruction. Earlier posterior vitrectomy, aphakia, glaucoma filtering or shunt surgery, iris or pupil irregularity, extensive synechiae, and shallow anterior chamber can affect EK success.

document_sections.heading: Penetrating Keratoplasty
document_sections.content: PK failure commonly follows rejection in the first few years or endothelial failure later. EK has more primary donor failures than PK because donor tissue undergoes more manipulation; after the initial learning curve, reported overall endothelial loss appears comparable between DSAEK and DMEK. Graft dislocation is specific to EK and repositioning can add tissue trauma. Rejection occurs after full- or partial-thickness grafting. The Swedish Corneal Transplant Registry reported 13% rejection over 1 year for PK in Fuchs dystrophy and PBK. One DSAEK study reported 6.0%, 14.0%, and 22.0% at 1, 2, and 3 years; another reported 7.6% at 1 year and 12.0% at 2 years. Two direct studies found no statistically significant PK-versus-DSAEK rejection difference in Fuchs dystrophy and PBK, whereas large cohorts reported significantly less rejection with DMEK than with PK or DSAEK. Reported graft survival for both PK and DSAEK at 5 years was 95% for Fuchs dystrophy and 73% for PBK. Endothelial decompensation was the leading failure cause for both. Traumatic wound rupture and ocular surface complications causing PK failure are uncommon with EK; EK may also reduce delayed surface healing and irregularity in patients with dry eye or blepharitis. DSAEK or DMEK is increasingly considered when a PK graft develops endothelial decompensation. EK-specific interface opacity or donor-button wrinkling may reduce correctable distance acuity and prompt regrafting. PK commonly causes ametropia and irregular astigmatism: average postoperative astigmatism was 4 to 6 diopters (D) up to 1 year, compared with 1.50 D total cylinder after DSAEK, of which 0.40 to 0.60 D was surgically induced. DSAEK-induced hyperopia averaged 1.10 D, with a range of 0.70 to 1.50 D. Its more predictable optical result assists IOL calculation; DMEK generally causes minimal hyperopic shift and permits less variable IOL-power adjustment. TABLE 3 compares short-term surgical outcomes for edema associated with Fuchs dystrophy and PBK, including graft events, rejection, vision, refraction, and endothelial loss.

document_sections.heading: Endothelial Keratoplasty
document_sections.content: Before 2000, nearly all transplant candidates with decompensated corneas underwent PK. The 2022 Eye Bank Association of America report indicated that approximately 62% of United States keratoplasties were EK and 32% were PK; it also indicated that 95% of patients with Fuchs dystrophy received EK. DLEK was constrained by stromal-interface optical imperfections and difficult dissection. DSEK and DSAEK instead replace recipient Descemet’s membrane with a donor lenticule containing posterior stroma and Descemet’s membrane; DSEK tissue is usually manually prepared and DSAEK tissue microkeratome-precut. The DSAEK lenticule can induce hyperopia, which matters when subsequent DSEK is likely after cataract surgery. DMEK replaces diseased Descemet’s membrane and endothelium with corresponding donor tissue in mild to moderate edema. EK is accepted as reducing long-term rejection risk while hastening visual recovery and improving optics (II-, Insufficient, Discretionary). DMEK represented 47% of United States EK procedures in 2021. Cataract extraction often precedes or accompanies EK. DMEK requires less IOL-power adjustment than DSAEK, although induced corneal astigmatism still limits calculation accuracy. Relative to PK, EK offers quicker recovery, more predictable refraction, smaller stable wounds, and lower rejection risk; PK-type suture and wound problems are rare, whereas EK can involve graft decentration or dislocation, rebubbling, acute angle-closure glaucoma, and interface problems. In DMEK, orientation markings and SF6 gas have significantly reduced iatrogenic primary graft failure and rebubbling; preloaded donor tissue eases insertion. DMEK is a leading option for standard endothelial failure when anterior-chamber visibility is good. DSAEK remains a leading option when visibility is reduced or the eye has prior glaucoma surgery or iris defects, although DMEK may also be considered. Ultrathin DSAEK tissue is <100 µm thick and has shown some visual-recovery benefit over standard DSAEK with similar complication and refractive outcomes. Nanothin DSAEK is <50 µm thick and may yield DMEK-like results, but remains an additive procedure rather than true tissue replacement. Eye banks usually prepare EK donor tissue; skilled preparation makes the slightly greater wastage associated with DMEK negligible.

document_sections.heading: Descemet’s Stripping Only/Descemet’s Stripping without Endothelial Keratoplasty
document_sections.content: Primary descemetorhexis, with or without a topical Rho kinase inhibitor, has been performed successfully for Fuchs dystrophy but not PBK. It removes a central 4 to 5 mm region of diseased Descemet’s membrane and endothelium without donor transplantation. Candidates require localized central disease and peripheral endothelial density of at least 1,000 cells/sq mm. Visual rehabilitation may take up to 6 weeks, and honeycomb-appearing edema may arise during healing. Ex vivo expansion of injectable endothelial cells remains under investigation.

document_sections.heading: Medical Management of Corneal Opacification
document_sections.content:
Care has two phases: treating the initiating cause, such as infection or trauma (I-, Moderate, Strong), and addressing resulting epithelial erosions, irregularity, scarring, thinning, and vascularization. This guideline emphasizes the second phase. Persistent nonhealing epithelial defects often precede opacity. Conventional care uses an antibiotic drop or ointment against secondary bacterial infection, selected with regard to local flora, contact lens history, immune status, and underlying illness. Assess waking blink and nighttime lid closure when a defect persists; temporary tarsorrhaphy using botulinum toxin or sutures may help if either is inadequate. A study found that pressure patching did not improve comfort or healing speed. A BCL or amniotic membrane may aid delayed healing. Oral doxycycline, topical Nacetylcysteine, and medroxyprogesterone inhibit matrix metalloproteinases and have been studied for persistent epithelial and stromal defects with varying results; in vivo benefit is difficult to assess. Autologous serum, cord blood tears, and platelet-rich plasma have shown benefit for persistent epithelial defects, but preparation requirements restrict access. Nerve growth factor has shown efficacy for nonhealing defects with neurotrophic keratopathy. Cenegermin 20 µg/ml 6 drops daily for 8 weeks, with follow-up to 24 to 48 weeks, produced higher corneal-healing rates than vehicle. substance P with insulin-like growth factor-1, fibronectin, and thymosin beta 4 have shown some benefit in selected cases but remain investigational.

Amniotic membranes may be placed as an onlay protective covering or an inlay tissue substitute. Their proposed healing effect involves the release of anti-inflammatory, anti-angiogenic, and healing-related mediators. Membranes mounted on scleral rings or supplied as wafers for placement beneath a bandage contact lens permit office-based use. Progressive corneal thinning or a small perforation generally needs structural reinforcement with tissue adhesive. A thin application of adhesive, such as cyanoacrylate, over a small area of severe thinning or an early descemetocele may remain attached for 6 weeks or longer when the underlying surface is clean and compact. Peripheral application may provide definitive treatment; central or paracentral application can permit repair without an emergency operation. A leaking descemetocele may require temporary sealing with an anterior-chamber air bubble while adhesive is placed. The application site must be dry and free of epithelium. Adhesive works best for a small impending perforation at the base of a crater rather than a bulging descemetocele. Described application tools include a 30-gauge needle, the wooden end of a cotton applicator, and a micropipette. Only enough adhesive to seal or support the defect should be used. Ocular use of tissue adhesive lacks U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval despite longstanding use; a sterile preparation is advisable to limit secondary infection. Fibrin glue should not be used for corneal perforations or descemetoceles because it breaks down before healing is complete. A bandage contact lens helps retain the adhesive and improve comfort. Topical corticosteroids are commonly used against intraocular and corneal inflammation. Long-term use calls for monitoring intraocular pressure and cataract development. Whether they limit scarring after resolution of an acute or subacute process remains uncertain. Studies of acute corneal ulcers generally found little improvement in healing or visual acuity, although the Steroids for Corneal Ulcers Trial found some benefit for central bacterial ulcers with worse initial acuity, except when Nocardia was responsible. Agents used against scarring after glaucoma or refractive surgery—mitomycin-C [MMC], 5-fluorouracil, tacrolimus, octreotide, and pirfenidone—have either produced epithelial surface toxicity at commonly used doses or have not been assessed for anti-scarring effects in corneal disease. Surface irregularity, as well as the opacity itself, often contributes to reduced vision. When irregularity is important, an RGP lens, or a hybrid or scleral lens when greater stability is needed, often improves vision and may avoid a more invasive procedure. Trial fitting with spectacle overcorrection can demonstrate potential improvement. Painted contact lenses and scleral shells can conceal an opacity when visual potential is poor. A scleral shell is particularly suited to reduced orbital volume or phthisis bulbi; a painted lens with a transparent pupillary area and opaque periphery can serve patients with peripheral opacities.

document_sections.heading: Surgical Management of Corneal Opacification
document_sections.content: The corneal layer or layers affected determine the operative approach. Table 4 relates the depth and representative causes of opacity to available procedures.

document_sections.heading: Epithelial Debridement
document_sections.content: Disease located anterior to Bowman’s layer, including epithelial basement membrane dystrophy and recurrent erosions, can be treated by removing epithelium until a smooth, reflective Bowman’s layer is visible. A therapeutic bandage contact lens and prophylactic topical antibiotics are commonly used afterward. A brief course of topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAID) drops may relieve discomfort, but close observation is needed because topical NSAIDs raise concern for corneal melting or perforation. Some lesions warrant additional techniques.

document_sections.heading: Management of Subepithelial Fibrosis
document_sections.content: Subepithelial fibrosis occurs with conditions such as Salzmann nodular degeneration and apical nodules in keratoconus. If debridement leaves an uneven stromal surface or a subepithelial lesion adheres firmly, a corneal burr or PTK can smooth the surface and lessen optical aberrations. Adjunctive MMC may be used to prevent or treat fibrosis or haze when recurrence risk is high.

document_sections.heading: Management of Band Keratopathy
document_sections.content: Band keratopathy involves hydroxyapatite deposits on the anterior Bowman’s layer and epithelial basement membrane associated with inflammation, local injury, or systemic hypercalcemia. It usually causes no symptoms, so debridement is reserved for glare, impaired vision, or pain caused by epithelial disruption. Deposits may be removed mechanically, chemically, or by combining both approaches: forceps can lift thick plaques, while finer material may require epithelial debridement followed by ethylene-diamine-tetra-acetic acid (EDTA) chelation. Studies support the safety and efficacy of alternative compounded EDTA sources where access is difficult. EDTA concentration and exposure time vary with calcium density and technique. A comparison reported mean healing times of 5–7 days after EDTA chelation versus 2–3 days for a similarly sized abrasion in normal eyes. Limiting EDTA exposure, including at the limbus, might hasten re-epithelialization. Slow healing increases the risk of stromal scarring and infection. When limbal stem cell deficiency, neurotrophic keratopathy, or severe dry eye coexists, amniotic membrane grafting or temporary tarsorrhaphy may support healing. With severe ocular surface disease, keratectomy risks may exceed its benefits. PTK is another option, but calcium ablates faster than adjacent tissue and may leave surface depressions and irregularities.

document_sections.heading: Management of Anterior Stromal Opacities
document_sections.content: Anterior lesions extending past Bowman layer into anterior or middle stroma need more extensive removal than superficial lesions. Anterior segment OCT, UBM, or confocal microscopy can help select the depth, diameter, and method of dissection.

document_sections.heading: Anterior Lamellar Keratectomy
document_sections.content: Several operations can remove visually important anterior stromal opacities. A freehand lamellar keratectomy requires little equipment but may leave an irregular surface that limits vision; an excimer laser, femtosecond laser, or microkeratome may produce a better refractive surface and acuity. Excimer laser PTK removes a preset depth of superficial or anterior stromal tissue. Methylcellulose or sodium hyaluronate can mask depressions around irregularities or deposits to avoid reproducing the uneven contour and to improve the postoperative refractive surface. Tissue removal also flattens the cornea and causes a hyperopic shift; small-spot ablations around the treatment-zone edge or a refractive setting can reduce that change. Visual improvement is related to corneal clarity, surface regularity, and optical quality. Reports of microkeratome or femtosecond keratectomy, alone or combined with PTK, describe significant improvement in final bestcorrected visual acuity [BCVA] and contrast sensitivity. In most cases, uncorrected visual acuity (UCVA) does not improve significantly at 6 months, whereas BCVA improves significantly at 2-, 6-, and 12-month assessments after mechanical or femtosecond flaps combined with PTK. Limitations of lamellar keratectomy include recurrence, postoperative irregularity, and haze. MMC has been studied for reducing recurrent scars or stromal deposits; PTK can also be repeated. In granular and lattice corneal dystrophies, PTK may postpone DALK or PK but can produce haze. Ectasia is another risk, especially when ablation exceeds the anterior third of corneal stroma or leaves a stromal bed less than 250 µm. Epithelial disruption permits infectious keratitis. Herpes virus belongs in the differential diagnosis because excimer exposure, corticosteroids, and corneal trauma can reactivate it; a history of herpetic eye disease warrants strong consideration of perioperative antiviral prophylaxis. Delayed epithelial healing may reflect the underlying disorder, and autologous serum or selfretained, glued, or sutured amniotic membrane may assist healing. A superficial corneal flap combined with excimer ablation of its stromal bed is another approach to deeper opacity.

document_sections.heading: Use of Mitomycin-C
document_sections.content: Superficial or anterior lamellar keratectomy can be followed by haze, which tends to resolve, or scarring, which persists and affects vision. Risk factors include dystrophy, delayed epithelial recovery, and ablation deeper than 50 to 75µm. When postoperative anti-inflammatory treatment may not adequately prevent scarring, intraoperative MMC can help. Mitomycin-C is an alkylating agent that suppresses activation and proliferation of wound-healing cells at the operative site. Its cytotoxic effect is used off-label to prevent or treat corneal scars, but it can deplete keratocytes or cause endothelial failure or limbal stem cell deficiency. Pharmacy preparation of the intended dose and careful control of exposure time are important. Definitive indications and the best technique, dose, and application duration for corneal disorders remain undetermined.

document_sections.heading: Corneal Tattooing
document_sections.content: Corneal tattooing has been used for cosmetic treatment of leukomas and to block visually troublesome iridotomies or other iris defects. Sterile commercial India ink or carbon particles are introduced into anterior or middle stroma by a method resembling stromal puncture, or through a manually or femtosecond-created lamellar pocket or flap. Pigment color and density differ among cases.

document_sections.heading: Keratoplasty
document_sections.content: Corneal transplantation is a principal treatment for opacity in the middle or deep stroma. Compared with PK, partial-thickness grafts offer substantially lower risks of graft rejection and traumatic wound rupture.

document_sections.heading: Lamellar Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty
document_sections.content: Anterior lamellar keratoplasty replaces part of the corneal thickness. Developing techniques aim to make the stromal interface clearer and improve vision.

document_sections.heading: Therapeutic Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty
document_sections.content: Automated lamellar therapeutic keratoplasty supplies structural support after corneal melting, including central ulcers, peripheral ulcerative keratitis, or Terrien marginal degeneration, or after peripheral ectasia, including pellucid marginal degeneration or postPK wound thinning. It is especially relevant when thinning is severe or a descemetocele forms. Central graft size and circular shape are chosen according to defect size and whether the edge would cross the pupil. Peripheral disease may need a concentric ring-shaped or partial crescent graft; some cases require a full-thickness patch or crescent. ALTK donor tissue may be partial-thickness irradiated, glycerin preserved, or otherwise preserved tissue supplied by an eye bank.

document_sections.heading: Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty
document_sections.content: DALK removes all or almost all stroma to restore vision in deep stromal opacity or scarring, corneal ectasia, or keratolysis associated with ocular surface disease or infectious keratitis; it can also follow earlier ocular procedures. Preserving host Descemet’s membrane and endothelium maintains a closed globe, lowering risks of intraoperative expulsive hemorrhage and traumatic wound rupture and shortening recovery. It also eliminates endothelial rejection and permits a lower topical steroid burden, although stromal rejection remains possible. Graft survival is longer than with PK, an important consideration for younger recipients. DALK is technically more difficult than PK. Host trephination can be manual or femtosecond-assisted. Laser-generated interlocking graft–host cuts may aid healing and stromal dissection. Methods of separating posterior stroma include the Melles stromal pocket, Anwar’s big-bubble technique, and manual dissection. Donor fixation uses suturing approaches similar to PK.

document_sections.heading: Outcomes
document_sections.content: Most DALK–PK comparisons concern keratoconus; the guideline considers their findings potentially applicable to central opacities that are noninflammatory, nonvascularized, and nonprogressive. After DALK, thicker residual host posterior stroma and greater donor–host interface reaction correlate with more variable acuity and contrast sensitivity. Studies report vision comparable to PK when Descemet’s membrane is fully exposed, but experienced surgeons achieved such exposure in only 47% to 82% of eyes. Descemet’s membrane perforation may necessitate conversion to PK; the need may diminish with surgeon experience. Studies found significantly less endothelial cell loss after DALK without membrane perforation than after full-thickness transplantation. For corneas with more than 1 quadrant of deep vascularization, ocular surface disease, concurrent glaucoma, or peripheral anterior synechiae, graft survival is significantly longer with DALK than PK. Table 5 compares survival at Year 1, Year 5, and Year 10 across overall, high-risk, and low-risk groups. At 10 years, survival was greatest for keratoconus, followed by post-infectious scarring, and poorest for inflammatory disease such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome or ocular cicatricial pemphigoid. A small study found no statistically significant DALK–PK differences in higher-order aberrations, objective/ocular scatter index, optical-quality measures, or corneal cylinder. Another study found no significant difference in patient quality of life a year or more after the two procedures.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: DALK complications include suture abscesses, epithelial erosions, interface scars or opacity, infectious keratitis, neovascularization, and stromal graft rejection or failure; endothelial rejection does not occur. Descemet’s membrane can rupture during stromal separation, particularly when scarring reaches the membrane or a previous spontaneous or operative rupture has occurred. Deeper scars increase perforation risk. A small rupture may allow completion of DALK, whereas a large one may require PK. Continuing lamellar surgery despite a larger perforation can permit fluid between membrane and graft, creating a double anterior chamber. Membrane detachment can also develop later with endothelial repopulation or traction from progressive fibrosis. Studies associate residual stroma less than 80 µm with better DALK vision and report acuity equivalent to PK after complete membrane exposure. Overall allograft rejection was 1.9% with DALK versus 7.8% with PK. Reported stromal rejection after DALK ranged between 2% and 12% and is usually reversible with topical corticosteroids. Endothelial loss follows intraoperative injury, especially with membrane perforation, then a chronic decline of about 3.9% annually, above physiologic loss. Post-DALK infection may involve sutures, unhealed epithelium, organisms trapped at the interface, or postoperative endophthalmitis; bacterial, atypical bacterial, and fungal pathogens are generally responsible. Interface infection generally needs surgery to clear donor–host infiltrates, either donor-button exchange or PK. In therapeutic DALK for Acanthamoeba keratitis, forming a big bubble was more difficult and infection recurred in 20% of cases; confocal microscopy or a wide margin around involved tissue are proposed to help avoid these outcomes. Graft failure was reported up to about 60%, chiefly because of inadequate endothelial function.

document_sections.heading: Indications
document_sections.content: The purpose of PK varies with the underlying disease. Improving vision is its most frequent indication; restoring support to a thinned or perforated cornea is another major indication.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric keratoplasty
document_sections.content: Eye Bank Association of America data indicate that pediatric corneal grafts are performed most often for ectasia or thinning, followed by congenital opacity; worldwide, infectious keratitis and chemical or mechanical injury are also indications. Overall health, available support, and whether opacity is unilateral or bilateral affect operative timing. The critical interval for visual development extends from 2 to 6 months after birth and is shorter with unilateral than bilateral media opacity. Pediatric corneal ophthalmologists favor intervention at 1 to 3 months of age. One study including unilateral and bilateral cases, however, found no difference in acuity or graft survival between transplantation at age 0 to 90 days and age 3 to 12 months. Amblyopia treatment matters for optimal results, and co-management with a pediatric optometrist or ophthalmologist is recommended.

document_sections.heading: Alternative Types of Keratoplasty
document_sections.content: Special PK approaches include crescentic patch grafts and rotational autografts. Peripheral opacity with tissue loss and astigmatism but a clear central cornea may call for an oval or crescent, partial- or full-thickness graft. An ipsilateral rotational full-thickness autograft can move a central scar into the far periphery; the graft–host junction must not approach the pupil closely enough to distort vision. Eccentric placement frequently produces irregular astigmatism and limits this technique. Oversized or tectonic grafts are used for substantial peripheral thinning or infection when disease extends outside the central 7.5 to 9.0 mm. Some patients receive an eccentric reinforcing patch first and conventional PK through that thickened tissue months later. Concurrent anterior-segment reconstruction may include angle repair, pupilloplasty, lensectomy, or IOL repositioning. When opacity blocks retinal surgery, a temporary plastic or silicone keratoprosthesis may provide a view during the vitreoretinal operation and then be exchanged for a full-thickness graft; its view is usually better than that through a newly transplanted cornea. Autokeratoplasty, reserved for functionally monocular patients, transfers clear cornea from a blind eye to an opaque eye with visual potential. Femtosecond laser-assisted keratoplasty cuts donor and recipient tissue into top-hat, mushroom, or zigzag configurations. Their larger wound interface might improve wound strength and healing, allowing earlier suture removal and quicker visual recovery; top-hat cuts additionally preserve more host endothelium. Studies found less early postoperative astigmatism with FLAK than conventional PK, but no significant difference by 6 months. Higher-order aberration measures favored FLAK for visual quality. Availability, logistics, expense, and absent insurance reimbursement limit femtosecond use.

document_sections.heading: Outcomes
document_sections.content: Graft clarity and visual improvement vary greatly by indication. For an avascular central scar without other ocular damage, reported graft clarity is well over 90%; extensive vascularization and limbal stem cell damage after chemical injury are associated with poor success. Limbal stem cell deficiency therefore needs treatment before keratoplasty. Cataract, glaucoma damage, or retinal disease can also determine postoperative acuity. Astigmatism after transplantation remains variable and difficult to predict. Surgeons often retain sutures long term after selective removal produces good vision with little astigmatism, but later suture breakage can cause irritation, infection, or rejection.

document_sections.heading: Contraindications
document_sections.content: Treating active or accompanying problems before corneal transplantation improves its prospects. Important measures include controlling intraocular pressure, resolving adnexal or intraocular inflammation and infection, and correcting eyelid abnormalities that cause exposure or other damage. Areas of thinning that create graft–host thickness mismatch, deep stromal blood vessels that increase rejection risk, and ocular surface disease—including dry eye, prior chemical or radiation injury, OMMP, or Stevens-Johnson syndrome—can reduce graft survival.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: The guideline distinguishes complications arising during surgery from those developing after it.

document_sections.heading: Intraoperative
document_sections.content: Reported intraoperative problems include scleral perforation by a fixation suture, incorrect trephination, damage or loss of donor tissue, retention of Descemet’s membrane, iris injury, loss or damage of the lens, lens dislocation, posterior capsule rupture with or without vitreous loss, hemorrhage in the anterior chamber or vitreous, posterior vitreous pressure, and suprachoroidal hemorrhage.

document_sections.heading: Postoperative
document_sections.content: Reported postoperative problems include rejection; graft-interface separation or graft displacement; irregular astigmatism; primary or late graft failure; leaking or misaligned wounds; persistent epithelial defects; filamentary keratitis; immune infiltrates, infection, or abscess related to sutures; cataract; endophthalmitis; increased intraocular pressure; blepharoptosis; anterior synechiae; hyphema; choroidal or retinal detachment; IOL dislocation; and lamellar-interface infection. Primary graft failure means that donor tissue has not cleared within the first 8 weeks after surgery without another explanation for stromal edema, such as persistent epithelial defect, raised pressure, rejection, or inflammation. Inadequate endothelial function from cell damage or too few cells is suspected; donor selection, preparation, storage, or excessive operative handling may contribute. Regrafting is generally required. Endophthalmitis after PK is uncommon but severe. Organisms may come from periocular inoculation, postoperative surface or interface defects, donor tissue, or storage medium. Routine donor-rim cultures poorly predict bacterial endophthalmitis, and fungal cultures have low positive predictive value for infection; fungal cultures may nevertheless be considered, while clinical findings direct management. Late graft failure develops years after transplantation and is thought to reflect progressive endothelial loss, possibly accelerated by rejection, infection, traumatic iritis, or elevated pressure. Donor manipulation during surgery, anterior-chamber shallowing after wound separation, and graft repositioning or rubbing after EK may also contribute to early loss of function. Rejection reactions are the most frequent cause of graft failure. Prompt intensive topical, periocular, and systemic corticosteroids may reverse endothelial rejection. Patients at high risk or with recurrent inflammation, including herpes simplex virus keratitis, herpes zoster ophthalmicus, or uveitis, may need greater daily corticosteroid doses or oral antivirals than standard post-PK protocols. Two studies comparing PK with DSAEK in Fuchs dystrophy and PBK found no statistically significant rejection-rate difference. More recent studies suggest that implanting less allogenic tissue, as with EK, lowers long-term rejection risk. Long-term topical corticosteroids may reduce rejection but call for surveillance for pressure elevation and infectious keratitis, including infection crystalline keratitis. EK became more common than PK in the United States in 2012. Reports documented fungal infection increasing from 0.014% in a 2013 report to 0.023% in a 2016 report. Studies found that three quarters of companion grafts had positive rim cultures when a fungal donor-rim culture was positive, and two thirds of recipients of culturepositive companion tissue developed infection. Fungal culture results should therefore be shared with the supplying eye bank to enable closer monitoring of the other recipient. There is no consensus on prophylactic antifungal therapy after a positive fungal culture, and antifungal additives to cold corneal-storage media remain under investigation.

document_sections.heading: Keratoprosthesis
document_sections.content: Artificial-cornea development has continued for well over 100 years, beginning with glass. Designs of particular interest include Cardona, osteo-odonto-keratoprosthesis, AlphaCor, and Boston keratoprosthesis. Boston type 1 keratoprosthesis (BKPro), the most frequently used artificial cornea, received FDA approval in 1992 initially for patients poorly suited to other corneal grafts, such as those with severe bilateral blindness after repeated graft failure. Its subsequent uses include trauma, herpetic keratitis, aniridia, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, limbal stem cell deficiency, silicone-oil-filled eyes, neurotrophic keratopathy, and extensive corneal neovascularization. BKPro uses a full-thickness graft with a central polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) optic; optical power is available in 1 diopter increments according to recipient axial length. It offers potential vision when other transplant types are unsuitable. Reported acuity reached 20/200 or better in 50% to 65% of patients at 3 years, with device retention of 80% to 87.8% at last follow-up; quality-of-life measures also improved significantly. Reported retention at 1 year, 2 years, and 5 years was 90% to 92%, 80% to 88%, and 74%, respectively. In autoimmune disease such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome or mucous membrane pemphigoid, retention may fall to 37.5% to 55%. Because the optic does not biologically integrate, its persistent junction with tissue can cause nonhealing epithelial defects, sterile necrosis, and perforation. Threats to globe integrity increase endophthalmitis risk, so lifelong antimicrobial prophylaxis is recommended. A typical BKPro regimen uses daily polymyxin B with trimethoprim or a fourth-generation fluoroquinolone, with or without vancomycin. High-risk patients with autoimmune disease or monocular vision need daily dual coverage: vancomycin with polymyxin B/trimethoprim or a fourth-generation fluoroquinolone, or a fluoroquinolone with chloramphenicol. Suspected fungal infiltrates on the therapeutic contact lens or prosthesis stem warrant immediate cessation of topical corticosteroids and treatment with natamycin 5%, amphotericin B, or voriconazole 1%. Therapeutic soft bandage contact lenses routinely limit surface desiccation and microtrauma and improve retention. For limbal stem cell deficiency, additional therapies deserve particular attention, especially after chemical injury, in autoimmune cicatricial conjunctivitis, or with herpes zoster, because anatomical and functional outcomes tend to be worse. Preoperative limbal stem cell transplantation, mucous membrane grafting, or amniotic membranes may improve the ocular surface (II++, Moderate, Discretionary). Successful concurrent conjunctival flaps have also been reported. Glaucoma is the leading cause of permanent vision loss associated with BKPro. Reports indicate pre-existing glaucoma in 72% to 89% of recipients, newly developed glaucoma in 14% to 36%, and progression in 13% to 33%. Progressive angle closure and chronic intraocular inflammation contribute. Because pressure is difficult to measure reliably after implantation, a low target estimated by finger palpation is advised. After tube-shunt surgery before or alongside implantation, one report found glaucoma progression as low as 2% over 17 months in eyes with poorly controlled pressure; other reports reached 38%, particularly when autoimmune ocular surface disease and other comorbidities were included. Repeated optic-nerve and visual-field assessment is needed. Other complications include hypotony, inflammation, and retroprosthetic membranes; Table 6 summarizes reported complication incidences. Postoperative complication incidence tended to fall significantly over the first 10 years among BKPro recipients treated for previous graft failure. Care may require glaucoma and retinal specialists. Long-term comparisons with PK are unavailable. Children are not ideal BKPro recipients, particularly for initial treatment. Boston type 2 keratoprosthetic may be an option when advanced ocular surface disease makes type 1 unsuitable; it entails complete tarsorrhaphy with the PMMA optic protruding through the eyelid. Osteo-odonto-keratoprosthesis has also had some success in Stevens-Johnson syndrome and OMMP.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up Evaluation
document_sections.content: Urgency varies widely with corneal edema or scarring. New or worsening pain, redness, photophobia, or visual symptoms may signal surface disruption, infection, inflammation, recurrence, or progression and warrant immediate medical attention. Prompt diagnosis and treatment help limit complications. Clinical judgment determines visit intervals both during diagnostic assessment and after medical or operative intervention. In corneal opacity, follow-up assesses clarity and surface irregularity; coexisting intraocular inflammation and intraocular pressure, including treatment-related changes, require regular reassessment.

document_sections.heading: PROVIDER AND SETTING
document_sections.content: An outpatient ophthalmologist is well placed to diagnose many causes of corneal edema or opacity, and comprehensive ophthalmologists may also provide medical treatment within their expertise. Infants and young children sometimes need examination under anesthesia to obtain information for treatment planning. Superficial keratectomy and excimer laser PTK can often be performed in an office or minor-procedure suite; most other operations need operating-room facilities and sterile conditions.

document_sections.heading: COUNSELING AND REFERRAL
document_sections.content: After diagnosis and work-up, patients should receive a detailed explanation of the cause and treatment choices. Consultation with a corneal specialist is recommended when diagnostic or medical needs exceed the treating clinician’s training or comfort or when complex surgery may be needed. Retina, glaucoma, or pediatric ophthalmic referrals may also be appropriate. Once disease resolves or stabilizes, care can return to the comprehensive ophthalmologist. Team care can be especially useful when travel to subspecialists is difficult, and the primary care physician should participate in discussions, particularly about surgery. Complex disease or treatment warrants thorough counseling so patients understand care challenges, develop suitable expectations, and make informed decisions.

document_sections.heading: SOCIOECONOMIC CONSIDERATIONS
document_sections.content: Globally, corneal opacity ranks fifth among causes of bilateral blindness. Of the 7 to 9 million people with bilateral corneal blindness, 90% live in low- or middle-income countries. Major causes include bacterial, fungal, viral, and parasitic keratitis and ocular trauma; limited access to care can further increase post-traumatic infection. Public-health infrastructure and primary eye-care investment support prevention, and nearly 80% of corneal blindness is avoidable. Corneal disease is associated with poverty and markedly shorter life expectancy, especially for children who are blind from corneal disease. Primary-health efforts in low- and middle-income countries address trachoma, onchocerciasis, vitamin A deficiency, and ophthalmia neonatorum. Obtaining and preparing donor tissue, establishing eye banks, and specialized preparation with a microkeratome or femtosecond laser add transplant costs, which must be weighed against the societal cost of preventable or correctable blindness. Compared with cataract blindness, corneal blindness affects younger people more often, including during productive and child-rearing years, and therefore entails substantial disability-adjusted life years beyond what prevalence alone indicates.

document_sections.heading: APPENDIX 1. QUALITY OF OPHTHALMIC CARE CORE CRITERIA
document_sections.content: The physician’s central ethical duty is to provide quality care in the patient’s best interests. Ophthalmologists should combine clinical skill and compassion, maintain and assess their competence through learning, arrange needed care or referral, support prevention, and respect patients’ dignity and vulnerability. Effective care rests on a patient–physician partnership: listening to concerns and explaining diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment in a way that supports informed participation and adherence. Clinical judgment should guide the choice and timing of tests, treatment, and follow-up according to urgency and individual needs. Clinicians should perform procedures only when appropriately competent or assisted, and should ensure timely access, continuity, arrangements for preoperative and postoperative care, and alternative care during absences. Referral and consultation should reflect patient needs, clinician expertise, availability, and timely exchange of adequate clinical information. Accurate records and timely review of consultations and laboratory findings are required. Patients without further effective treatment should receive appropriate support, rehabilitation, social services, counseling, and referral. Before invasive testing or treatment, relevant history and examination should inform a truthful discussion of diagnosis, proposed and alternative options, their purposes, risks, benefits, likelihood of success, and the consequences of no treatment. New technologies should be adopted judiciously in view of cost, comparative benefit, safety, and efficacy. Ophthalmologists should review their performance, share clinically important knowledge and unexpected complication patterns, use facilities capable of handling urgent ocular or systemic complications, and pursue cost-effective care without unacceptable loss of quality.

document_sections.heading: APPENDIX 2. INTERNATIONAL STATISTICAL CLASSIFICATION OF DISEASES AND RELATED HEALTH PROBLEMS (ICD) CODES
document_sections.content: The appendix lists ICD-10 CM classifications for corneal edema and associated entities, and for minor, peripheral, central, and phthisical corneal opacity. Some ICD-10 CM categories require a 7th character, which must occupy the 7th position; when necessary, X fills unused preceding positions. For bilateral disease without a bilateral code, separate right- and left-eye codes should be assigned. An unspecified code is reserved for situations without another coding option. When a diagnosis code specifies laterality, right corresponds to 1, left to 2, and bilateral to 3, irrespective of whether this appears in the 4th, 5th, or 6th digit.

document_sections.heading: APPENDIX 3: DETERMINATION OF INTRAOCULAR PRESSURE IN DISEASED OR POSTSURGICAL CORNEAS
document_sections.content: Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT) alone can estimate intraocular pressure (IOP) inaccurately in a diseased or surgically altered cornea. Changes in thickness, hydration, curvature, astigmatism, epithelial regularity, or stromal scarring alter its subjective endpoint; alternative measurement methods are therefore strongly advised. A pneumotonometer uses airflow resistance against a conforming 5-mm fenestrated silicone tip, generates 40 readings per second, measures ocular pulse amplitude, and requires topical anesthesia. A non-Goldmann applanation device has a 1-mm transducer and surrounding cornea-flattening ring; it collects 500 samples per second, averages 8 or 10 readings within confidence limits, and requires topical anesthesia. An ocular response analyzer applies an air pulse to measure corneal hysteresis and derive corneal-compensated and GAT-equivalent pressure, also measures ocular pulse amplitude, and does not require topical anesthesia. The slit-lamp-mounted Pascal dynamic contour tonometer samples pressure 100 times per second through a concave, contour-matching tip intended to minimize corneal-property effects. It reports pressure and ocular pulse amplitude after 6 seconds or 6 ocular pulse cycles and requires topical anesthesia. Rebound tonometry calculates pressure from a plastic-tipped metal probe striking the cornea at 0.25 m/sec, with contact lasting approximately 0.05 sec; Six measurements are needed, and anesthesia is unnecessary. The handheld Mackay-Marg tonometer combines applanation and indentation, electronically measures pressure through a small plunger, averages repeated readings, and requires topical anesthesia. Although corneal properties influence applanation and rebound methods more than some alternatives, these methods may estimate pressure more accurately and reproducibly than GAT across changes in corneal disease. The same valid method should be used at successive visits to detect meaningful pressure rises and begin treatment before irreversible optic-nerve injury. Disease- or treatment-related pressure elevation may otherwise escape detection with GAT alone.

document_sections.heading: LITERATURE SEARCHES FOR THIS PPP
document_sections.content: PubMed searches were conducted on March 3, 2022, with limited updates on June 7, 2023. Filters targeted human, English-language randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews, with date limits for publications since June 27, 2018. The panel assessed 973 studies and included 42. Searches combining the disease with patient values or patient preferences found no results. An economic-evaluation and treatment-cost search found 33 studies; all 33 were provided to the panel, and none qualified for inclusion. The documented searches covered medical and surgical management, transplantation, diagnosis, pathology, physiology, physiopathology, socioeconomic issues, and patient values. The study-selection diagram records n = 973 identified and assessed, n = 931 excluded, and n = 42 included.

conditions.name: Corneal edema
conditions.description: Excess fluid accumulates in one or more corneal layers. Causes include endothelial dysfunction, elevated intraocular pressure, inflammation, trauma, dystrophies, infection, hypoxia, surgery, and toxicity.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Vision may be blurred or fluctuate, often worsening on waking and improving later in the day. Photophobia, redness, tearing, foreign-body sensation, and pain may occur. Onset is usually gradual, although pressure elevation, substantial inflammation, and hydrops can produce a more acute presentation. Peripheral disease may cause few symptoms, while central involvement generally affects vision; functional disability can exceed that suggested by standard visual acuity.

subtypes.name: Corneal edema due to wearing contact lenses
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Contact lens use is the identified cause.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish onset, fluctuation, laterality, symptoms, effects on daily activities, and potential causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Morning blur that clears later may accompany endothelial dysfunction; visual acuity alone may understate glare-related disability.

diagnostic_workup.test: Visual acuity, pinhole testing, manifest refraction, and glare testing
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure visual loss, best-corrected potential, and functional impairment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial evaluation; assessment of visual potential is particularly important before surgery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Functional status and measured acuity need not agree.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the lids and ocular surface; distinguish epithelial from stromal edema; identify guttae, epithelial breakdown, inflammation, scarring, Descemet’s membrane abnormalities, deposits, and other potential causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial evaluation and subsequent assessment as clinically indicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Sectoral edema with keratic precipitates or an anterior chamber reaction can point toward endotheliitis. Inferior edema can accompany retained material or a foreign body in the inferior angle.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify pressure elevation or hypotony contributing to edema.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Evaluation and monitoring, particularly when pressure-related disease or corticosteroid treatment is relevant.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Goldmann applanation tonometry may be unreliable in an abnormal cornea. Alternative methods include a pneumotonometer, handheld electronic applanation tonometer, dynamic contour tonometer, ocular response analyzer, rebound tonometer, and digital palpation; consistent use of the same valid method supports serial comparison.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess posterior-segment conditions associated with hypotony and secondary edema when examination warrants it.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When posterior-segment assessment is needed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Chronic serous choroidal detachment or retinal detachment may contribute through hypotony.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Look for retained lens fragments, foreign bodies, or iridocorneal adhesions.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When angle pathology or retained material is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Findings can help establish the cause of localized edema.

diagnostic_workup.test: Potential acuity meter or illuminated near-card pinhole testing
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate visual potential despite anterior-segment pathology.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly before a surgical treatment decision.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Better performance than on conventional acuity testing supports the possibility of improvement after treatment; a poor result does not necessarily establish poor visual potential.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether surface irregularity substantially contributes to visual loss.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When edema or scarring disturbs the central or paracentral surface.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Improvement with the lens, but not with spectacles, favors surface irregularity as a major contributor.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure corneal thickness and assess serial change.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When endothelial function or progression requires assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Serial thickness measurements can help assess endothelial function. Measurements from different device types are not directly interchangeable.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess irregular astigmatism, corneal thickness, posterior-surface findings, and the depth of associated opacification.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When evaluating visual impairment, prognosis, or surgical planning.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Peripheral pathology may create visually important central irregularity.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess endothelial cell density, shape, and uniformity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When endothelial assessment can contribute to evaluation or serial monitoring.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Cell imaging does not directly measure endothelial function or reserve; diffuse confluent guttae can prevent useful imaging.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Image corneal layers and investigate endothelial, stromal, or infectious causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly helpful in unilateral edema or when specular imaging is limited by moderate edema.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Characteristic appearances may help identify iridocorneal endothelial syndrome, epithelial or fibrous ingrowth, PPCD, fungal hyphae, or Acanthamoeba cysts.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Image corneal and retrocorneal structures, measure thickness, and assess surgical anatomy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When deeper structural pathology is suspected or after endothelial keratoplasty.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Can reveal a detached Descemet’s membrane, retrocorneal membrane, stromal cleft, or an area where donor tissue has not adhered.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine anterior-segment structures despite opacity and locate small foreign bodies.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Especially useful in congenital or traumatic cases and for surgical planning.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Can show displaced or ruptured Descemet’s membrane, adhesions, and retrocorneal membranes.

follow_up.schedule: Visit intervals depend on clinical judgment, improvement or stability, and the intervention performed. A bandage contact lens used for an extended period requires regular review and periodic replacement; in most cases, the same lens should not remain for longer than one month.
recommended_tests: Serial pachymetry when monitoring endothelial function
Intraocular pressure assessment when pressure elevation or corticosteroid response is a concern
Reassessment of the ocular surface, symptoms, and contact lens fit when a bandage contact lens is used
long_term_effects: Persistent endothelial damage may cause edema to recur years after an initially resolving injury.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: New or worsening pain, redness, photophobia, or vision changes warrant prompt medical attention.

conditions.name: Corneal opacification
conditions.description: Corneal transparency is reduced by material within one or more layers, such as fluid, scar tissue, inflammatory debris, or metabolic deposits. Causes span congenital, degenerative, dystrophic, inflammatory, metabolic, infiltrative, neoplastic, postsurgical, and traumatic conditions.
conditions.epidemiology: Globally, corneal opacity is the fifth leading cause of bilateral blindness. Of the 7 to 9 million people with bilateral corneal blindness, 90% live in low- to middle-income countries; nearly 80% of corneal blindness is avoidable.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Visual impairment may arise from both the opacity and surface irregularity. Central involvement usually produces symptoms; peripheral lesions can be subtle but may induce central irregularity and astigmatism. Infectious opacity often begins acutely, whereas most noninfectious deposition or scarring develops gradually. Most noninflammatory opacities persist.

subtypes.name: Peripheral corneal opacity
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Peripheral pathology may cause central irregularity and visually significant astigmatism.

subtypes.name: Central corneal opacity
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Involvement of the pupillary region generally produces symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.test: History and assessment of daily activities
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize onset, symptoms, laterality, functional impairment, and ocular, systemic, medication, trauma, contact lens, family, and exposure histories.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An acute presentation can suggest infection; most noninfectious deposition and scarring evolve more gradually.

diagnostic_workup.test: Visual acuity, pinhole testing, manifest refraction, glare testing, and potential acuity testing
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure visual disability and estimate the potential for improvement.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial evaluation; potential acuity assessment is important before surgery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A poor potential acuity result does not necessarily rule out visual improvement.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the ocular surface, eyelids, opacity location and depth, epithelial integrity, inflammation, deposits, scarring, thinning, and vascularization.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial evaluation and clinically indicated follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The affected corneal layer is important in selecting a surgical approach.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Separate the visual effect of an irregular refractive surface from that of the opacity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When surface irregularity may contribute to reduced vision.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Vision that improves over an RGP lens but not spectacles suggests that irregularity is a major contributor.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document surface irregularity and irregular astigmatism.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When determining the source of visual impairment or planning treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Irregular keratometry mires correlate with surface irregularity.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess opacity depth, corneal thickness, and anatomy relevant to surgical planning.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When the extent of disease or a procedure needs evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Light-based measurements lose accuracy and resolution as opacity or stromal edema increases.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Image stromal deposits and investigate infectious organisms.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When microscopic characterization may guide diagnosis or treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Fungal hyphae and Acanthamoeba cysts may have recognizable appearances.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Define scar or deposit depth and identify concealed structural abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When evaluating deeper disease or planning surgery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: May show pathology concealed by corneal scarring.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate opacity depth and anterior-segment structures when light-based imaging is limited.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly in congenital or traumatic disease and surgical planning.

diagnostic_workup.test: Intraocular pressure measurement and fundus examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess concomitant ocular disease and visual prognosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As part of comprehensive examination and subsequent monitoring.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Corneal abnormalities can make Goldmann applanation measurements unreliable.

follow_up.schedule: Intervals depend on clinical judgment and whether the condition is improving or stable.
recommended_tests: Assessment of corneal clarity and surface irregularity
Regular reassessment of coexisting intraocular inflammation and intraocular pressure
follow_up.survivorship_notes: New or worsening pain, redness, photophobia, or vision changes can signal surface disruption, infection, inflammation, recurrence, or progression and require prompt evaluation.

conditions.name: Fuchs dystrophy
conditions.description: An endothelial corneal dystrophy associated with guttae and a risk of corneal edema and endothelial decompensation.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Edema can cause morning visual blur, glare, and distortion even when measured acuity remains relatively good. Disease affecting the central cornea generally causes symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate endothelial disease and look for guttae or edema.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of suspected endothelial dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Diffuse, confluent guttae can limit the usefulness of specular microscopy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor corneal thickness as an indicator of changing endothelial function.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When diffuse guttae are present or progression is a concern.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Serial change is more informative about function than a single endothelial cell image.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess patterns that may predict endothelial decompensation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Prognostic assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Irregular isopachs, displacement of the thinnest point, and focal posterior-surface depression may indicate greater risk, independently of pachymetry measurements.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess endothelial cell characteristics when cells can be imaged.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As an adjunct to clinical examination and pachymetry.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It does not directly measure endothelial function or reserve and may add little when guttae are diffuse and confluent.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate a variant associated with the dystrophy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Additional evidence is needed before genetic testing can be recommended for clinical management. A small prospective study found a significant association between allele repeats and corneal clearance after Descemet’s stripping only, but could not predict time to clearance.

pathology_markers.expected_result: Diffuse or confluent endothelial guttae may be visible.
pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Their presence supports evaluation of endothelial dysfunction and can impede specular imaging.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: This variant in the transcription factor 4 gene results in a CTG triplet repeat expansion strongly associated with Fuchs corneal dystrophy; its role in clinical management remains insufficiently established.

recommended_tests: Tomographic evaluation when monitoring endothelial disease
long_term_effects: Endothelial decompensation may affect future visual function and planning of cataract surgery.

conditions.name: Pseudophakic or aphakic bullous keratopathy
conditions.description: Bullous corneal disease associated with the pseudophakic or aphakic state; the guide addresses its visual impairment, pain, and corneal transplantation outcomes.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Epithelial bullae can produce discomfort or pain. With longstanding bullous disease, a subepithelial scar may form and be accompanied by fewer bullae and less pain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine edema, bullae, epithelial integrity, scarring, and anterior-segment anatomy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial assessment and treatment planning.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The extent of subepithelial or stromal scarring influences the choice of transplant procedure.

diagnostic_workup.test: Visual acuity and potential acuity assessment
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine visual disability and the potential value of rehabilitation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before selecting treatment, especially surgery.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify pressure-related contributions to edema.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial assessment and follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Abnormal corneas can make Goldmann applanation measurements less reliable.

recommended_tests: Assessment of symptoms, epithelial integrity, and corneal clarity
Intraocular pressure assessment when clinically indicated
long_term_effects: Longstanding disease may lead to subepithelial scarring.

conditions.name: Keratoconus – hydrops
conditions.description: An acute corneal edema presentation associated with keratoconus and an endothelial or Descemet’s membrane break.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Unlike the typically gradual presentation of corneal edema, hydrops may begin acutely. A large Descemet’s membrane break and a central stromal cleft may be present.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess acute edema and the corneal structures involved.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Acute presentation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Image Descemet’s membrane and the stromal architecture.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When characterizing hydrops or planning management.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: May reveal a substantial Descemet’s membrane break and central stromal cleft.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine Descemet’s membrane and anterior-segment anatomy when needed.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When additional structural assessment is required.

recommended_tests: Monitoring for improvement and resolution of edema

conditions.name: neurotrophic keratopathy
conditions.description: The guide discusses this condition in relation to persistent epithelial defects and impaired corneal-surface healing.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A nonhealing epithelial defect may precede opacity associated with infection, inflammation, tissue breakdown, or scarring.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify and follow a persistent corneal epithelial defect.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When healing is delayed.

diagnostic_workup.test: Assessment of blinking and eyelid closure
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify inadequate surface protection that may impede epithelial healing.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Whenever an epithelial defect persists.

conditions.name: Band keratopathy
conditions.description: Hydroxyapatite accumulates along the anterior surface of Bowman’s layer and the epithelial basement membrane; inflammation, local injury, or systemic hypercalcemia may contribute.
conditions.clinical_presentation: It is usually asymptomatic but can cause glare, visual disability, or pain when the epithelium is disrupted.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess calcium deposits, their density, and epithelial disruption.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Evaluation of suspected band keratopathy or its symptoms.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Symptoms and epithelial damage help determine whether removal should be considered.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify conditions that may delay healing after deposit removal.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before a procedure.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Limbal stem cell deficiency, neurotrophic keratopathy, and severe dry eye may complicate re-epithelialization.

pathology_markers.expected_result: Deposits on the anterior aspect of Bowman’s layer and the epithelial basement membrane.
pathology_markers.clinical_significance: The deposits account for the corneal band.

recommended_tests: Assessment of re-epithelialization and signs of stromal scarring or infection after treatment
long_term_effects: Delayed healing after deposit removal can increase the risk of stromal scarring and infection.

conditions.name: Salzmann nodular degeneration
conditions.description: A corneal degeneration discussed as a cause of subepithelial fibrosis and opacity.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Peripheral disease may be subtle or asymptomatic, although induced central irregularity and astigmatism can affect vision. An adherent subepithelial lesion or an irregular surface after epithelial removal can complicate treatment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify the subepithelial lesion and examine the corneal surface.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Clinical assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess visually significant surface irregularity and astigmatism.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When visual symptoms or treatment planning warrant it.

recommended_tests: Assessment of surface regularity and recurrent fibrosis or haze when treated

conditions.name: Epithelial basement membrane dystrophy
conditions.description: An epithelial corneal dystrophy included among the causes of opacity; lesions anterior to Bowman’s layer are addressed in the discussion of epithelial debridement.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The guide identifies it in the context of superficial epithelial lesions and recurrent erosions.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the epithelium and determine the superficial location of the lesion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Evaluation of an epithelial lesion or recurrent erosion.

conditions.name: Granular corneal dystrophy
conditions.description: A corneal dystrophy that can produce opacity extending into the anterior or mid stroma.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Opacity can cause substantial glare or functional impairment even when visual acuity is 20/40 or better.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the opacity and identify the affected corneal layers.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Clinical evaluation.

diagnostic_workup.test: Corneal topography and RGP contact lens over-refraction
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate whether surface irregularity contributes to visual impairment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When measured acuity does not adequately explain visual function or surgery is being considered.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Improvement over the lens suggests that irregularity contributes substantially.

diagnostic_workup.test: Anterior segment OCT, UBM, or confocal microscope
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Define lesion depth and extent to guide stromal surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When operative planning requires it.

recommended_tests: Assessment for recurrence, haze, and surface irregularity after lamellar treatment
long_term_effects: The underlying dystrophy may recur after treatment.

conditions.name: Lattice corneal dystrophy
conditions.description: A corneal dystrophy discussed among causes of opacity that may be treated with phototherapeutic keratectomy before a later transplant becomes necessary.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the opacity and affected corneal layers.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Clinical evaluation.

diagnostic_workup.test: Anterior segment OCT, UBM, or confocal microscope
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess stromal lesion depth for surgical planning.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When more extensive excision is being considered.

recommended_tests: Assessment for recurrent opacity or postoperative haze when treated
long_term_effects: The underlying dystrophy can recur after lamellar treatment.

conditions.name: limbal stem cell deficiency
conditions.description: An ocular-surface condition that can impair healing and compromise the outcome of procedures for corneal opacity.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify surface disease relevant to epithelial healing and transplantation planning.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before keratectomy, keratoplasty, or keratoprosthesis when surface compromise is a concern.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Severe ocular-surface disease can make keratectomy risks outweigh its benefits; deficiency associated with a chemical injury should be addressed before keratoplasty.

recommended_tests: Assessment of epithelial healing and ocular-surface stability
long_term_effects: Ocular-surface compromise can reduce corneal graft survival.
